citations.quote: **(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every $p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive diagonal entries.
An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$.

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector $n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$.
$\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite.

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field $n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that $n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly, $$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$ Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing.

**(c) Tetrad fields.** A **tetrad field** (or **$g$-orthonormal frame field**) on $U$ is a local frame field $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$ such that $$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\eta_{AB}\qquad\text{for all }A,B\text{ and all }q\in U .$$ A tetrad field is **future-directed** when in addition $E_0(q)$ is future-directed for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]); then each $E_0(q)$ is an observer at $q$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so $E_0$ is an observer congruence on $U$ ([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]), while $E_1,E_2,E_3$ are pointwise an orthonormal basis of the rest space of that observer.
**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for $(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and $g$-compatible.

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]), $$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$ on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and $$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$ For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with $$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

derivations.claim: In a chart, $\partial_a\widetilde g_{bc}=\Omega^2(\partial_ag_{bc}+2u_ag_{bc})$ and $\widetilde g^{ad}=\Omega^{-2}g^{ad}$. Substituting these into the Christoffel formula [F3] cancels the common $\Omega^2$ and gives $\widetilde\Gamma^a{}_{bc}-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=C^a{}_{bc}:=\delta^a_bu_c+\delta^a_cu_b-g_{bc}u^a$, where $u^a=g^{ab}u_b$. The reciprocal $\Omega^{-1}$ is smooth on the positive range by [F6], and $d\Omega$ is a smooth one-form by [F5], so $u$ and $C$ are smooth.

By [F5], $0=d(1)=d(\Omega^{-1}\Omega)=\Omega^{-1}d\Omega+\Omega\,d(\Omega^{-1})$, so $d(\Omega^{-1})=-\Omega^{-2}d\Omega$. Therefore $du=d(\Omega^{-1})\wedge d\Omega+\Omega^{-1}d^2\Omega=-\Omega^{-2}d\Omega\wedge d\Omega=0$. Torsion freedom in [F3] gives $(du)_{ab}=\nabla_a u_b-\nabla_bu_a$, hence $H_{ab}=H_{ba}$.

Expanding the curvature definition [F2] with $\widetilde\Gamma=\Gamma+C$ gives $\widetilde R^a{}_{bcd}-R^a{}_{bcd}=
abla_cC^a{}_{db}-
abla_dC^a{}_{cb}+C^a{}_{ce}C^e{}_{db}-C^a{}_{de}C^e{}_{cb}$. Indeed, the terms linear in $C$ from the coordinate curvature formula are its partial derivatives plus the $\Gamma C$ terms; grouping them by the tensor covariant-derivative rule in [F4] yields the two $
abla C$ terms, while the remaining terms are the displayed quadratic products.

Contracting $a$ with $c$ as in [F2], the derivative terms are $
abla_aC^a{}_{db}-
abla_dC^a{}_{ab}$. The definition of $C$ gives $C^a{}_{ab}=4u_b$ and, using $
abla g=0$ from [F4], $
abla_aC^a{}_{db}=H_{db}+H_{bd}-g_{db}	heta=2H_{bd}-g_{db}	heta$ by step 2.1. Thus their difference is $-2H_{bd}-g_{bd}	heta$.

The first quadratic contraction is $C^a{}_{ae}C^e{}_{db}=4u_e(\delta^e_du_b+\delta^e_bu_d-g_{db}u^e)=8u_bu_d-4g_{bd}s$. Expanding the second contraction into its nine terms gives $C^a{}_{de}C^e{}_{ab}=u_du_b+u_du_b-g_{db}s+4u_du_b+u_du_b-u_du_b-u_du_b-g_{db}s+u_du_b=6u_bu_d-2g_{bd}s$. Their difference is $2u_bu_d-2g_{bd}s$. Combining this with step 3.1 proves the Ricci transformation in the Statement.
Contracting the Ricci transformation with $\widetilde g^{ab}=\Omega^{-2}g^{ab}$ gives $\widetilde S=\Omega^{-2}(S-2\theta-4\theta+2s-8s)=\Omega^{-2}(S-6\theta-6s)$.

By definition, $\widetilde G_{ab}=\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ab}-\tfrac12\widetilde S\,\widetilde g_{ab}$. Substituting the Ricci formula from step 4.1 and $\widetilde S\,\widetilde g_{ab}=(S-6\theta-6s)g_{ab}$ from step 5.1 cancels the scalar-curvature terms and leaves $G_{ab}-2H_{ab}+2u_au_b+2g_{ab}\theta+g_{ab}s$. This is the claimed Einstein-tensor formula.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the bounded linear operators on $H$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); for $M\in\mathcal B(H)$, $M^*$ is its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

Under this same $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis, [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]] gives $M^*\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $\|M^*\|=\|M\|$.

A **finite bounded Kraus instrument datum** on $H$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, integers $q_a\ge0$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$, and bounded operators $M_{a,r}\in\mathcal B(H)$ for $r=1,\ldots,q_a$. It is **normalized** when

$$\sum_{a=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H.$$

Empty inner sums are zero. For each outcome $a$, define its outcome operator and operation by

$$E_a:=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad \mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*\quad(X\in\mathcal B(H)).$$

These formulas take values in $\mathcal B(H)$: the adjoint theorem above makes each $M_{a,r}^*$ bounded, and $\|M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*x\|\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|X\|\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\,\|x\|=\|M_{a,r}\|^2\,\|X\|\,\|x\|$; the sums are finite. This definition specifies only the displayed finite Kraus form; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary instruments and does not assert that an apparatus realizes these data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

derivations.claim: For each $a,r$, $M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ is self-adjoint because $\langle M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}x,y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}y\rangle$, and its quadratic form is $\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\ge0$. Hence $E_a\ge0$. Normalization gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}\sum_rM_{b,r}^*M_{b,r}\ge0$, including empty sums, so $E_a$ is an effect.

By [F7], each $M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ is trace class, so the finite sum $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is trace class. For all $x,y\in H$, $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,y\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}^*x,\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle$ because $\rho=\rho^*$ and $M_{a,r}^*$ is the Hilbert adjoint. Also $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$. Finite summation shows $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint and positive.

By [F1], write $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ in trace norm. For its partial sums $\rho_N=\sum_{j\le N}w_jT_{u_j,u_j}$, [F7] gives $\|M_{a,r}(\rho-\rho_N)M_{a,r}^*\|_1\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|\rho-\rho_N\|_1\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\to0$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathcal J_a(\rho)=\sum_{r,j}w_jT_{M_{a,r}u_j,M_{a,r}u_j}$ in trace norm; the trace-norm sum is finite since $\sum_jw_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\le\|M_{a,r}\|^2\sum_jw_j=\|M_{a,r}\|^2$ for each $r$. Trace continuity [F5] and [F3] yield $p_a=\sum_{r,j}w_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\ge0$. Cyclicity [F2] gives $p_a=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$.

Because the outcome and Kraus index sets are finite, [F1] and step 2.1 give $\sum_ap_a=\sum_jw_j\langle(\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jw_j\|u_j\|^2=1$ by normalization. Since every $p_a\ge0$, this also gives $p_a\le1$ for every $a$.

If $p_a>0$, step 1.2 gives a positive trace-class numerator $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ and step 2.1 gives its trace $p_a$, so $\rho_a=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is positive trace class with trace one, hence a density operator by [F1]. The finite sum $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is likewise positive trace class, and its trace is $\sum_ap_a=1$ by step 3.1, so it is a density operator. If $p_a=0$, division by $p_a$ is undefined and no normalized update is asserted.

For a unit vector $\psi$, [F3] gives that $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace $\|\psi\|^2=1$, hence a density operator by [F1]. Also [F4] gives $M_{a,r}T_{\psi,\psi}M_{a,r}^*=T_{M_{a,r}\psi,M_{a,r}\psi}$. Taking traces and summing over the finite Kraus list yields $p_a=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$, as claimed.
Each $n!$ is a finite complex number, so the sequence $(n!)_{n\ge0}$ defines an element $S(g)=\sum_{n\ge0}n!g^n$ of $\mathbb C\llbracket g\rrbracket$ by [A1], irrespective of numerical convergence.

Fix any $g\ne0$ and put $t_n=n!g^n$. Then $|t_{n+1}|/|t_n|=(n+1)|g|$, which is greater than $2$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $|t_n|$ eventually grows by a factor greater than $2$ at every step, so $t_n$ does not tend to zero.

If the numerical series $\sum_nt_n$ converged, its partial sums $s_N:=\sum_{n=0}^Nt_n$ would converge, so $t_n=s_n-s_{n-1}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$; step 1.2 rules this out for every nonzero $g$. At $g=0$, the convention $g^0=1$ leaves only the constant term, so the series equals $1$. Thus the series converges at no nonzero $g$. For every $r>0$, the point $g=r/2$ lies in $|g|<r$ and gives divergence, so no positive $r$ satisfies the defining property of the radius; $r=0$ satisfies it vacuously. Therefore $R=0$ and the claimed positive radius fails.

derivations.claim:
Fix $k,m\ge0$, write $n=k+m$, and let $\psi_m\in K_s^{(m)}$. Expanding
the permutation average and using symmetry of $\psi_m$ gives
$P_{s,n}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m)=\binom nk^{-1}\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\|I|=k}}v_I$, where $v_I$ is the tensor with $e$ in the slots in $I$ and the $m$ factors of
$\psi_m$ in the remaining slots, symmetrized there. Indeed, for each fixed
placement $I$, the $k!m!$ permutations of the equal $e$ factors and the
symmetric $\psi_m$ give the same tensor, and
$k!m!/n!=\binom nk^{-1}$.

Distinct placements $v_I$ are orthogonal: if $I\ne I'$, some slot contains $e$ in one tensor and a vector of $K$ in the other, and $e\perp K$. Each $v_I$ has norm $\|\psi_m\|$, so step 1.1 gives $\|P_{s,n}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m)\|^2 =\binom nk^{-1}\|\psi_m\|^2$. The same orthogonality shows that the images for different $k$ in a fixed $n$ sector are orthogonal. Thus the factor $\sqrt{\binom nk}$ makes $J_{k,m}$ isometric and their sector ranges are orthogonal.

Algebraic elementary tensors in $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ are dense by [F1]. Expand each factor using $H=\mathbb Ce\oplus K$, distribute the finite tensor product, and apply $P_{s,n}$. Every resulting term has exactly $k$ factors $e$ and $m=n-k$ factors in $K$, so it lies in the range described in step 2.1. Since $P_{s,n}$ is bounded and algebraic elementary tensors are dense, their symmetrizations are dense in $H_s^{(n)}$; the range of the isometry is closed, hence it equals $H_s^{(n)}$. Taking the orthogonal direct sum over $n=k+m$ proves that $J$ is onto and unitary.

On a vector $e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m$ with $n=k+m$, creation by $e$ acts by $\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(e\otimes J_{k,m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m))$. Since $P_{s,n+1}$ averages over all permutations, symmetrizing the last $n$ slots first does not change the result. This equals $\sqrt{n+1}\sqrt{\binom nk}P_{s,n+1}(e^{\otimes(k+1)}\otimes\psi_m)$. The binomial identity $\binom{n+1}{k+1}=\frac{n+1}{k+1}\binom nk$ makes this exactly $J_{k+1,m}(\sqrt{k+1}\,e^{\otimes(k+1)}\otimes\psi_m)$. Thus creation becomes the stated one-mode raising map. Annihilation by $e$ is zero for $k=0$, because every first tensor factor lies in $K$. For $k\ge1$, the placement formula of step 1.1 shows that contraction keeps exactly the $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ placements with $e$ in the contracted slot. Therefore $a(e)J_{k,m}\psi_m= \sqrt n\sqrt{\binom nk}\frac{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}{\binom nk} P_{s,n-1}(e^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\psi_m) =\sqrt k\,J_{k-1,m}\psi_m$, using $\binom nk=\frac nk\binom{n-1}{k-1}$. Thus annihilation becomes the stated one-mode lowering map and leaves the $K$ factor unchanged.
