Assume Countable Choice, the constants in [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], $\hbar>0$, and a finite integer $N\ge1$. Let the real configuration space be $Q=\mathbb R^{2N}$ with coordinates $(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_N,y_N)$ and let $T^*Q\cong\mathbb R^{4N}$ have corresponding real canonical momentum coordinates $(P^x_1,P^y_1,\ldots,P^x_N,P^y_N)$. On real smooth functions define the canonical Poisson bracket
$$\{F,G\}=\sum_{j=1}^N\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_j}\frac{\partial G}{\partial P^x_j}-\frac{\partial F}{\partial P^x_j}\frac{\partial G}{\partial x_j}+\frac{\partial F}{\partial y_j}\frac{\partial G}{\partial P^y_j}-\frac{\partial F}{\partial P^y_j}\frac{\partial G}{\partial y_j}\right),$$
and extend it $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to complex-valued smooth functions on $T^*Q$. Define the complex coordinate notation
$$z_j=x_j+iy_j,\qquad \bar z_j=x_j-iy_j,\qquad p_j=\frac{P^x_j-iP^y_j}{2},\qquad \bar p_j=\frac{P^x_j+iP^y_j}{2}.$$
These definitions give
$$\{z_j,p_k\}=\delta_{jk},\qquad \{\bar z_j,\bar p_k\}=\delta_{jk},$$
with all other elementary brackets zero; the bracket is extended by bilinearity and the Leibniz rule. The first-order kinetic term $\frac{i\hbar}{2}\sum_j(\bar z_j\dot z_j-\dot{\bar z}_jz_j)$ gives primary constraints
$$C_j=p_j-\frac{i\hbar}{2}\bar z_j,\qquad \bar C_j=\bar p_j+\frac{i\hbar}{2}z_j.$$
In the order $(C_1,\ldots,C_N,\bar C_1,\ldots,\bar C_N)$ their constraint matrix and inverse are
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\hbar I_N\\i\hbar I_N&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-iI_N/\hbar\\iI_N/\hbar&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Here, “second class” means that the constraint matrix $M_{AB}=\{\chi_A,\chi_B\}$ is invertible. Thus these constraints are second class. For a real smooth finite-mode Hamiltonian $H\in C^\infty(Q;\mathbb R)$, viewed as independent of the momenta, define the Wirtinger derivative
$$\frac{\partial H}{\partial\bar z_j}:=\frac12\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_j}+i\frac{\partial H}{\partial y_j}\right).$$
The Dirac bracket
$$\{F,G\}_D=\{F,G\}-\{F,\chi_A\}(M^{-1})_{AB}\{\chi_B,G\}, \quad \chi=(C_1,\ldots,C_N,\bar C_1,\ldots,\bar C_N),$$
satisfies $\{z_j,\bar z_k\}_D=-i\delta_{jk}/\hbar$ and $\{z_j,z_k\}_D=\{\bar z_j,\bar z_k\}_D=0$. For a real smooth finite-mode Hamiltonian $H(z,\bar z)$ the reduced equation is $i\hbar\dot z_j=\partial H/\partial\bar z_j$. These are ordinary commuting coordinates; they do not derive CAR by canonical quantization.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. Write
$$\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3:E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+\mathsf M^2}\}$$
for the positive shell in that Definition, and $C_+=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:E\geq|\mathbf q|\}$ for the closed future cone of $h=(+,-,-,-)$. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda(C_+)=C_+$. For energy four-vectors on these positive shells, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Let $\mathsf M_1,\mathsf M_2\geq0$, let $P$ be future timelike, meaning $P^0>0$ and $h(P,P)>0$, set $s=h(P,P)>(\mathsf M_1+\mathsf M_2)^2$, and write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2}$. For a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda_P$ with $\Lambda_P P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$, define the finite Borel measure $\Phi_{2,P}$ as the pushforward of $\frac{k_*}{16\pi^2\sqrt{s}}d\Omega$ under
$$\mathbf n\longmapsto\left(\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_1^*,k_*\mathbf n),\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_2^*,-k_*\mathbf n)\right),$$
where $E_i^*$ and $k_*$ are from [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The proof below shows that $\Phi_{2,P}$ is independent of the choice of $\Lambda_P$; for $P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ it is exactly the center-of-momentum measure $d\Phi_2$ in that Definition. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, for each fixed angular direction and nonnegative Borel radial function $g:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$, the radial action after spatial evaluation is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_{2,P}$. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\int d\Phi_{2,P}=\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_{2,P}=\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For the scattering flux identities, take incoming $p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)\in\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}}$, where $\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, and require $p_1+p_2=P$. A center-of-momentum map is a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$; write $\Lambda p_1=(E_1^*,\mathbf p_1^*)$ and define $p_*=|\mathbf p_1^*|$. The value is independent of the choice of $\Lambda$, since two such maps differ by a spatial rotation. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest, represented by $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$, and two equal-rest-energy daughters on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}$ with total four-vector $P_0$ and constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

Let $m,M\geq0$ be the electron and muon rest energies in joules. Use the positive shells of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]: $p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)$ with $E_i=\sqrt{|\mathbf p_i|^2+m^2}>0$ for $i=1,2$, and $k_i=(\varepsilon_i,\mathbf k_i)$ with $\varepsilon_i=\sqrt{|\mathbf k_i|^2+M^2}>0$ for $i=1,2$. With $p_1+p_2=k_1+k_2=P$, set $s=h(P,P)>4\max(m^2,M^2)$, using the algebraic metric $h=(+,-,-,-)$ of [[def-qft-example-data]]. Since $P^0=E_1+E_2>0$ and $h(P,P)=s>0$, $P$ is future timelike. A center-of-momentum map is a proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, $\Lambda(C_+)=C_+$ for $C_+=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:E\geq|\mathbf q|\}$, and $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$. Write $\mathbf p_1^*$ and $\mathbf k_1^*$ for the spatial components of $\Lambda p_1$ and $\Lambda k_1$, respectively. The strict threshold makes both nonzero; define $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ by $\cos\theta=(\mathbf p_1^*\cdot_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf k_1^*)/(|\mathbf p_1^*||\mathbf k_1^*|)$. This angle is independent of the chosen center-of-momentum map because any two choices differ by a spatial rotation. Use the dimensionless coupling $g=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}$ from [[def-qft-example-data]]. Adopt only the formal single-photon tree coefficient
$$\mathcal M=\frac{g^2}{s} [\bar v(p_2)\gamma^a u(p_1)] [\bar u(k_1)\gamma_a v(k_2)],$$
with equal weight $1/4$ on the four initial spin-label pairs and a sum over final spin labels. No interacting continuum $S$-matrix or exact QED cross section is assumed.

In the auxiliary finite-matrix setting of [L1], assume $d\geq1$, an invertible $K_0$, and the stated covariance of $K_0$ and $V$ under the finite-graph phase action; then the coefficientwise inverse and covariance identities in [L1] hold. Separately stipulate the displayed formal pair-production amplitude above. Its on-shell spin average is
$$\overline{|\mathcal M|^2} =g^4[3-\beta_e^2-\beta_\mu^2 +\beta_e^2\beta_\mu^2\cos^2\theta], \qquad \beta_e=\sqrt{1-\frac{4m^2}{s}}, \quad \beta_\mu=\sqrt{1-\frac{4M^2}{s}},$$
where the angle $\theta$ is defined above. The resulting formal differential and total coefficients are
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{\alpha^2(\hbar c)^2\beta_\mu}{4s\beta_e} [3-\beta_e^2-\beta_\mu^2+\beta_e^2\beta_\mu^2\cos^2\theta],$$
$$\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}} =\frac{\pi\alpha^2(\hbar c)^2}{s}\frac{\beta_\mu}{\beta_e} [3-\beta_e^2-\beta_\mu^2+\tfrac13\beta_e^2\beta_\mu^2].$$
If $\delta=4m^2/s\leq1/2$, the full differential coefficient divided by its $m=0$ value is between $1$ and $1+4\delta$. This bound concerns only omission of the incoming electron mass in this formal tree coefficient, not loop, soft-radiation, threshold, or empirical errors.

The same on-shell equations give $P_a\bar v(p_2)\gamma^a u(p_1)=0$ and $P_a\bar u(k_1)\gamma^a v(k_2)=0$. Thus a propagator term proportional to $P_aP_b$ does not change this specified tree coefficient. These current cancellations are proved locally for all $m,M\geq0$; the actual QFT-MG03 matrix-Ward carrier supplies only its finite-matrix inverse and covariance interface, not the broader tree-current clauses in the historical Q7 research module.

Let $m\geq0$ be a scalar rest energy in joules, and let $p_1,p_2,k_1,k_2$ be the incoming and outgoing scattering vectors on the positive $m$-shell of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]], so each $(E,\mathbf q)$ satisfies $E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+m^2}>0$. Require $p_1+p_2=k_1+k_2=P$ and $s=h(P,P)>4m^2$, with $h$ as in [[def-qft-example-data]]. Evaluate the coefficient map in a center-of-momentum frame $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ as defined in [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]]. For one scalar initial label of weight $1$ and one specified final channel, take the dimensionless real quartic tree amplitude $\mathcal A=-\lambda$. The coefficient map of [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]] gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{128\pi^2s}, \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}=\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{32\pi s}$$
for identical final scalars integrated over the full labeled sphere. For distinguishable final scalars the two coefficients are twice these values.

For a parent at rest, $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with energy $\mathsf M_0>2m$, decaying through a specified single channel to two identical scalars on the positive $m$-shell whose total four-vector is $P_0$, under a constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{coeff}} =\frac{|G_E|^2}{32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0} \sqrt{1-\frac{4m^2}{\mathsf M_0^2}}.$$
This result concerns the defined formal coefficients. It does not assert an exact exponential survival law.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. Write
$$\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3:E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+\mathsf M^2}\}$$
for the positive shell in that Definition, and $C_+=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:E\geq|\mathbf q|\}$ for the closed future cone of $h=(+,-,-,-)$. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda(C_+)=C_+$. For energy four-vectors on these positive shells, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Let $\mathsf M_1,\mathsf M_2\geq0$, let $P$ be future timelike, meaning $P^0>0$ and $h(P,P)>0$, set $s=h(P,P)>(\mathsf M_1+\mathsf M_2)^2$, and write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2}$. For a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda_P$ with $\Lambda_P P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$, define the finite Borel measure $\Phi_{2,P}$ as the pushforward of $\frac{k_*}{16\pi^2\sqrt{s}}d\Omega$ under
$$\mathbf n\longmapsto\left(\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_1^*,k_*\mathbf n),\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_2^*,-k_*\mathbf n)\right),$$
where $E_i^*$ and $k_*$ are from [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The proof below shows that $\Phi_{2,P}$ is independent of the choice of $\Lambda_P$; for $P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ it is exactly the center-of-momentum measure $d\Phi_2$ in that Definition. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, for each fixed angular direction and nonnegative Borel radial function $g:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$, the radial action after spatial evaluation is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. $$\int d\Phi_{2,P}=\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_{2,P}=\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For the scattering flux identities, take incoming $p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)\in\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}}$, where $\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, and require $p_1+p_2=P$. A center-of-momentum map is a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$; write $\Lambda p_1=(E_1^*,\mathbf p_1^*)$ and define $p_*=|\mathbf p_1^*|$. The value is independent of the choice of $\Lambda$, since two such maps differ by a spatial rotation. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest, represented by $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$, and two equal-rest-energy daughters on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}$ with total four-vector $P_0$ and constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. In the common natural-unit field convention, $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, a scalar field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and a Dirac field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation set $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, with $A_a$ in tesla-metres and gauge function $\chi$ in webers. With charge $q$ in coulombs define
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every radius $R>0$ and every
nonnegative Borel function $\varphi:[0,R]\to[0,\infty]$, with extended
Lebesgue integrals and the convention $0\cdot\infty=0$,
$$ \int_{\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\ |x|\le R\}}\varphi(|x|)\,d\lambda_4(x) =2\pi^2\int_0^R\varphi(r)r^3\,dr. $$
In particular, the radial Jacobian and angular factor on a four-dimensional
ball are $r^3$ and $2\pi^2$, respectively.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and let $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its bosonic Fock space and finite-particle domain.
For $h\in H$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the Segal field
$$\phi_0(h):=2^{-1/2}\bigl(a^\dagger(h)+a(h)\bigr).$$
For $h\ne0$, this symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint; write
$\Phi(h)=\overline{\phi_0(h)}$. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$,
$G=\mathcal F_s(K)$, choose a countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $G$
whose vectors are finite-particle, and use the one-mode splitting of
[[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]] followed by the Hermite unitary
$|n\rangle\mapsto g_n$ into $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with pairing
$\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$ to write a vector as
$(f_j)_{j\in J}\in\ell^2(J;L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C))$. Then the exact domain and
action are
$$D(\Phi(h))=\left\{(f_j):\sum_{j\in J}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+r^2x^2)|f_j(x)|^2\,dx<\infty\right\},\qquad (\Phi(h)f)_j(x)=rx f_j(x).$$
For $h=0$, $\phi_0(0)$ closes to the zero operator on all of $\mathcal F_s(H)$.

Define $\epsilon(z)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}z^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{n!}$ for $z\in H$.
There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by
$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
They obey
$$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$
and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. For every $h$, the one-parameter
group $t\mapsto W(th)$ has norm derivative at zero exactly on
$D(\Phi(h))$, with derivative $i\Phi(h)$ (for $h=0$ this is the zero
generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $m\ge1$, let U,V be open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, and let $T:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Borel $h:V\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_V h(y)\,dy=\int_U h(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,dx$, with equality in $[0,\infty]$ and $0\cdot\infty=0$. This statement concerns Borel h; no completed-measurable substitution is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim:
For every leg and $n\in S^2$,
$1-v_i\cdot n\ge1-|v_i|>0$. Since the leg set is finite, each summand of
$K(n)$ is continuous and bounded on $S^2$. Moreover
$$ h(K(n),(1,n))= \sum_i\eta_iQ_i\frac{1-v_i\cdot n}{1-v_i\cdot n} =\sum_i\eta_iQ_i=0. $$
Thus $K^0(n)=n\cdot\mathbf K(n)$ and
$h(K,K)=(K^0)^2-|\mathbf K|^2=-|P_T(n)\mathbf K(n)|^2$.
Consequently the angular integrand is nonnegative, bounded and measurable;
the coefficient $C$ is finite and nonnegative.

By [F6] and [F7], the $d\Omega$ used in the statement is the finite
Euclidean surface measure, and [F8] gives
$d^3q/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega)=
\omega\,d\omega\,d\Omega/(2(2\pi)^3)$. Multiplying by
$|h_\lambda(\mathbf q)|^2=g^2|K_\perp(n)|^2/\omega^2$ and integrating over
$\lambda<\omega<\Lambda$ gives
$$ \|h_\lambda\|^2= \frac{g^2}{2(2\pi)^3}\int_{S^2}|K_\perp|^2d\Omega \int_\lambda^\Lambda\frac{d\omega}{\omega} =C\log(\Lambda/\lambda). $$
The substitution $\omega=\lambda u$ and [F15] give the displayed logarithm.
The cutoffs are strictly positive and finite, so the norm is finite. The
endpoint set $\{\lambda,\Lambda\}$ is null by [F11], so the strict cutoff
convention gives the same integral as including either endpoint.

By [F10] at $p=2$, the real-valued scalar space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ has a countable dense set $D$. It is nonempty because this scalar $L^2$ space is nonempty and $D$ is dense. By [F12], $D\times D$ is at most countable; [F14] supplies a surjection from $\mathbb N$ onto this nonempty product. Composing with $(d,e)\mapsto d+ie$ and applying [F14] again shows that the nonempty set $D_{\mathbb C}:=\{d+ie:d,e\in D\}$ is at most countable. Every complex scalar $u\in L^2$ has real and imaginary parts $u_R,u_I\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$, and
$$\|u-(d+ie)\|_2^2=\|u_R-d\|_2^2+\|u_I-e\|_2^2.$$
Since $D$ is dense, for each $\varepsilon>0$ choose $d,e\in D$ with both squared errors less than $\varepsilon^2/2$; hence $D_{\mathbb C}$ is dense in complex scalar $L^2$. Applying [F12] twice, the nonempty product $D_{\mathbb C}^3$ is at most countable. It is dense in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$: for $z=(z_1,z_2,z_3)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, approximate each component by some $w_j\in D_{\mathbb C}$ with squared error less than $\varepsilon^2/3$, so the sum of squared errors is less than $\varepsilon^2$. For $n\in S^2$ and $z\in\mathbb C^3$, put $a=\sum_jn_jz_j$. Using [F13] and realness of $n_j$, direct expansion gives
$$\|P_T(n)z\|^2=\sum_j|z_j-n_ja|^2=\sum_j|z_j|^2-|a|^2\le\|z\|^2,$$
and $(I-nn^T)^2=I-nn^T$ because $\sum_jn_j^2=1$. Integrating the pointwise norm bound gives $\|M_{P_T}u\|_2\le\|u\|_2$, and the matrix identity gives $M_{P_T}^2=M_{P_T}$; hence this multiplier is a bounded idempotent on the ambient $L^2$ space. Given $z\in\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $w\in D_{\mathbb C}^3$ with $\|w-z\|_2<\varepsilon$. Contractivity and $M_{P_T}z=z$ give $\|M_{P_T}w-z\|_2\le\|w-z\|_2<\varepsilon$. The nonempty image $M_{P_T}(D_{\mathbb C}^3)$ is at most countable: [F14] gives a surjection from $\mathbb N$ onto $D_{\mathbb C}^3$, whose composition with $M_{P_T}$ surjects onto the image, so [F14] applies. This image is dense in the current space [F2], proving that space separable as required by [F4]. Define
$$ (Uh)(k)=\frac{\hbar c}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^3\,2|k|}}h(\hbar ck)\quad(k\ne0). $$
Set $Uh(0)=0$, which does not affect its $L^2$ class. The linear change $\mathbf q=\hbar ck$ has Jacobian $(\hbar c)^3$ by [F9], and $|\mathbf q|=\hbar c|k|$; substitution proves $\|Uh\|_{L^2(d^3k)}=\|h\|$. Its inverse is
$h(\mathbf q)=\sqrt{(2\pi)^3\,2|\mathbf q|}\,(\hbar c)^{-3/2}(Uh)(\mathbf q/(\hbar c))$, so $U$ is onto the ambient length-coordinate $L^2$ space. Both formulas
multiply by a nonzero scalar and scale the same spatial momentum by
$\hbar c>0$, so $\mathbf q\cdot h(\mathbf q)=0$ a.e. is equivalent to
$k\cdot(Uh)(k)=0$ a.e. Thus their restrictions give a unitary
$U:\mathcal H_{E,T}\to\mathcal H_T$, with the displayed inverse restricted
to $\mathcal H_T$. Since $K_\perp(n)$ is transverse, $Uh_\lambda$ belongs to the range in [F2]. Substitution of the formula for $h_\lambda$ gives exactly
$$ (Uh_\lambda)(k)=\mathbf1_{\{\lambda/(\hbar c)<|k|<\Lambda/(\hbar c)\}} |k|^{-3/2}\frac{gK_\perp(k/|k|)}{\sqrt{2(2\pi)^3}}. $$
Its angular coefficient has squared integral $C$ by the definition of $C$.

Put $N=N_\lambda$. The series for $\epsilon(f_\lambda)$ has squared
sector norms $N^m/m!$, so its total squared norm is $e^N$. Setting
$h=-i\sqrt2 f_\lambda$ and $z=0$ in [F4] yields
$W(h)\Omega=e^{-N/2}\epsilon(f_\lambda)$, hence $\Psi_\lambda$ is
normalized and its sector squared norms are
$s_m=e^{-N}N^m/m!$. The exponential series gives
$\sum_ms_m=1$ and, by shifting the index,
$\sum_m m s_m=N$. These are norm identities only; no measurement
interpretation is used.

On the support, the one-photon energy $\omega_\gamma(k)=\hbar c|k|$
satisfies $0<\omega_\gamma<\Lambda$. By [F5], the energy on sector $m$ is
the sum of its $m$ one-photon energies, bounded above by $m\Lambda$.
The same exponential series gives
$\sum_m m^2s_m=N^2+N<\infty$, so
$\sum_m\| (H_\gamma\Psi_\lambda)_m\|^2
\le\Lambda^2(N^2+N)$ and the vector lies in the operator domain.
For each $m\ge1$, the sector quadratic form of the unnormalized tensor
$f_\lambda^{\otimes m}/\sqrt{m!}$ is
$m\langle f_\lambda,\omega_\gamma f_\lambda\rangle
N^{m-1}/m!$. Summing with the factor $e^{-N}$ gives
$\langle\Psi_\lambda,H_\gamma\Psi_\lambda\rangle
=\langle f_\lambda,\omega_\gamma f_\lambda\rangle$. In energy coordinates
the latter integral is
$$ \frac{g^2}{2(2\pi)^3}\int_{S^2}|K_\perp|^2d\Omega \int_\lambda^\Lambda d\omega=C(\Lambda-\lambda). $$
This is a free-model Hilbert-space expectation in joules, not an empirical
measurement.

If $C=0$, the nonnegative integral defining $C$ gives $K_\perp=0$ almost
everywhere, so $h_\lambda=f_\lambda=0$ as Hilbert-space vectors and
$\Psi_\lambda=\Omega$. If $C>0$, the function
$b=gK_\perp/\sqrt{2(2\pi)^3}$ is a nonzero transverse member of
$L^2(S^2;\mathbb C^3)$, with squared norm integral $C$. Its cutoffs
$\epsilon=\lambda/(\hbar c)$ and $\kappa=\Lambda/(\hbar c)$ satisfy
$0<\epsilon<\kappa$, and step 3.1 identifies its exact wavefunction with
[L1]'s current family. Conditional on [L1], its weak-zero and no-strong-limit
claims apply, and its energy formula agrees with step 5.1 because
$\hbar cC(\kappa-\epsilon)=C(\Lambda-\lambda)$.

To prove the projective-ray claim separately, put
$\epsilon_j=\kappa2^{-j}$ and $f_j=f_{\epsilon_j}$. The increment
$f_{j+1}-f_j$ is supported on the disjoint shell
$\epsilon_{j+1}<|k|<\epsilon_j$, so its squared norm is
$C\log2>0$, using [F15] on this radial shell. Also
$\langle f_j,f_{j+1}\rangle=\|f_j\|^2$, because the increment is orthogonal
to $f_j$. By [F4] and the normalization in step 4.1,
$|\langle\Psi_j,\Psi_{j+1}\rangle|=e^{-C\log2/2}<1$. For every phase $\theta$,
$$ \|\Psi_{j+1}-e^{i\theta}\Psi_j\|^2 =2-2\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}\langle\Psi_j,\Psi_{j+1}\rangle) \ge2(1-e^{-C\log2/2})>0. $$
Thus adjacent rays remain a fixed positive projective distance apart, so
the ray sequence is not Cauchy and has no projective limit: phases making the unit vectors converge in norm to a fixed unit representative would force adjacent phase-adjusted differences to tend to zero, contradicting this uniform lower bound. This fills the
interface difference in [L1] without asserting that its current statement
contains a projective-ray result.

citations.quote: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In the selected model of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]], let $H_\mu$ be the scalar one-particle Hilbert
space and let $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ be the
Dirac particle/antiparticle one-particle space. Let $\Omega_s$ and $\Omega_D$
be their zero-particle Fock vectors. The assignments of $H_\mu$ to bosonic
Fock space and $\mathcal K$ to CAR Fock space are the physical assumptions
of that postulate.

For every unit scalar wave-packet mode $h\in H_\mu$, define
$$|n\rangle_h=\frac{(a^\dagger(h))^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\Omega_s,\qquad n\ge0.$$
These vectors are normalized and mutually orthogonal, belong to the
finite-particle domain, and
$$a(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle_h,\qquad a^\dagger(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle_h,$$
where $a(h)|0\rangle_h=0$. The maximal operator domains supplied by
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] are
$$D(a(h))=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n)\in\mathcal F_s(H_\mu):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n)\in\mathcal F_s(H_\mu):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Define the one-mode number operator as the composition
$$N_h:=a^\dagger(h)a(h),\qquad D(N_h):=\{\Psi\in D(a(h)):a(h)\Psi\in D(a^\dagger(h))\},\qquad N_h\Psi:=a^\dagger(h)(a(h)\Psi).$$
The displayed finite-particle vectors $|n\rangle_h$ belong to $D(N_h)$ and
satisfy $N_h|n\rangle_h=n|n\rangle_h$.

For every unit Dirac particle mode $u\in\mathcal H_+$ or antiparticle mode
$u\in\overline{\mathcal H_-}$, regarded as a vector of $\mathcal K$, the
bounded operator $N_u=c^\dagger(u)c(u)$ is an orthogonal projection. The
one-mode subspace generated by $u$ is the closed span of
$\{(c^\dagger(u))^n\Omega_D:n\ge0\}$. It is spanned by $\Omega_D$ and
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$; the latter is normalized and
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. Thus a single Dirac CAR mode has occupation $0$ or $1$.
All statements are conditional on the adopted representations and
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. They do not derive which statistics nature assigns to
all fields and do not assert an experimental observation.

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space $$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero components. For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is $a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$, bosonic annihilation is $a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$, fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction $c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and $c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]].
$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Adopt the following specified free-photon model in the oriented,
time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and length coordinates of
[[def-qft-framework-units]], with metric $(-,+,+,+)$ and $x^0=ct$. The
classical electromagnetic input is the smooth source-free branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]; the electromagnetic two-form and its potential
components are those of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and a supplied
potential is subject to [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. These EM suppliers
are physical input and conventions: they do not by themselves construct a
quantum representation.

For almost every $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, set
$\mathbf n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}$. The mathematical
definition [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]] specifies the positive
one-photon Hilbert space

$$\mathcal H_T= \{u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3): \mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\},$$

with the inherited pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$,
linear in the second variable as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The
value assigned to $P_T$ at
$\mathbf k=0$ is immaterial because that point has Lebesgue measure zero; no
continuous polarization frame over all momentum directions is chosen. Adopt
the bosonic Fock representation $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ and the free
Hamiltonian

$$H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|),$$

where on the $n$-photon sector $d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$ is multiplication by
$\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ and is zero on the vacuum sector. Its exact
self-adjoint domain and the unitary mass-cone action are those in the
mathematical supplier [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]]. The actual
smeared field-strength distributions and bounded Weyl operators are those
constructed in [[lem-qft-photon-local-weyl-observables]]; a pointwise
potential or field-strength operator is not asserted to exist. These
mathematical suppliers are draft carriers with mixed current Step 1 status: the
transverse-space, null-quotient, covariance-spectrum, framework-units, and
C01 measurement carriers have current ready records; the local-Weyl carrier is
escalated through its field-strength prerequisite. Readiness records are not
independent approval, and every use remains conditional on the exact statement
and proof supplied.

For the physical interpretation of an actually constructed state and a
supplied normalized measurement instrument, use
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]: Born probabilities are
assigned only to that specified model and instrument. This postulate records
the model's free Maxwell quanta as photons. It does not assert that the
model has been empirically confirmed, and it introduces no interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, LSZ limit,
asymptotic completeness, or nonperturbative continuum limit. In calculations
using an indefinite four-polarization auxiliary space, only the positive
transverse model or its separately constructed null quotient is physical;
four auxiliary components are not four positive photon states.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Work in the fixed length coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf w$; write $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$. For subsets $S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, say they are **spacelike separated** when $\eta(x-y,x-y)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(x^0-y^0)^2>0$ for every $x\in S$ and $y\in T$. Let $A_0=0$ and let $A_i$ be the transverse potential operator-valued distribution of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]]. Set
$$F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,\qquad E_i=-\partial_0A_i,\qquad B_i=\epsilon_{irs}\partial_rA_s,$$
where $\epsilon_{irs}$ is the totally antisymmetric symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. In the commutator formulas below, $\Delta=\sum_{r=1}^3\partial_r^2$ is the spatial Laplacian acting on $x-y$.
For a real antisymmetric test tensor $h=(h^{ab})$ with $h^{ab}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ and $h^{ab}=-h^{ba}$, define
$$F(h)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}F_{ab}(x)h^{ab}(x)\,d^4x =-A_b(\partial_a h^{ab}).$$
The effective test is conserved, $\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$, and $F(h)$ is unchanged by $A_b\mapsto A_b+\partial_b\lambda$ for smooth $\lambda$. Its one-particle coefficient $g_h$ is the vector $g_j$ of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] for $j_i=-\partial_a h^{ai}$, so $F(h)=a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h)$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

Let $C_0=-i\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ is the massless scalar causal commutator of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. As distributions in $x-y$,
$$[E_i(x),E_j(y)]=[B_i(x),B_j(y)] =(-\delta_{ij}\Delta+\partial_i\partial_j)C_0(x-y),$$
$$[E_i(x),B_j(y)]=\epsilon_{jri}\partial_0\partial_rC_0(x-y).$$
Every right-hand side has support in the closed causal cone. Hence compactly supported tests whose supports are spacelike separated in the stated Minkowski sense give commuting field-strength operators on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The quotient representation of [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]] makes these smeared field strengths Lorentz covariant: their on-shell coefficient depends on a polarization class only through $p_a\epsilon_b-p_b\epsilon_a$. These conclusions concern gauge-invariant free observables and do not assert locality of the Coulomb potential.

Assume Countable Choice and use the Minkowski coordinates and separation condition of [[lem-qft-photon-local-field-strength]], so $\eta(x-y,x-y)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(x^0-y^0)^2$. A spacetime region $O$ means an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$ in its standard topology. A real antisymmetric test $h=(h^{ab})$ is supported in $O$ when each component $h^{ab}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ has support contained in $O$. Two open regions $O_1,O_2$ are spacelike separated when $\eta(x-y,x-y)>0$ for every $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$. Let $g_h\in\mathcal H_T$ be the one-particle vector for such a test from [[lem-qft-photon-local-field-strength]]. The space $\mathcal H_T$ is separable: it is the range of the bounded projection $P_T$ on the separable space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. Define
$$W_O(h)=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2\,g_h),$$
where $W_{\rm Segal}$ is the Weyl unitary of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. It is bounded and unitary, and its one-parameter group has the self-adjoint field-strength closure as generator. For every open region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, let $\mathcal A(O)$ be the norm-closed unital $*$-algebra generated by $W_O(h)$ for real antisymmetric tests supported in $O$; equivalently its bounded real and imaginary parts are included as observables. If $O_1,O_2$ are spacelike separated by the stated Minkowski condition, then $\mathcal A(O_1)$ and $\mathcal A(O_2)$ commute.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use

Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}$, so the effective Clifford metric is
$-\eta$. In a supplied free Dirac model the displayed equation is
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and

Assume Countable Choice. Let $j=(j_1,j_2,j_3)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ and use $\mathcal H_T$ and $P_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. For $\omega=|\mathbf k|$ and $\mathbf k\ne0$, define

Its matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology; it is an operator-valued distribution and does not assign a pointwise operator to $A_i(x)$. With $E_i=-\partial_0A_i$, the equal-time canonical commutator is the distribution
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)] =-i\,P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Work in the fixed length coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf w$; write $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$. For subsets $S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, say they are **spacelike separated** when $\eta(x-y,x-y)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(x^0-y^0)^2>0$ for every $x\in S$ and $y\in T$. For a real antisymmetric test tensor $h=(h^{ab})$ with $h^{ab}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ and $h^{ab}=-h^{ba}$, define
$$F(h)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}F_{ab}(x)h^{ab}(x)\,d^4x =-A_b(\partial_a h^{ab}).$$
The effective test is conserved, $\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$, and $F(h)$ is unchanged by $A_b\mapsto A_b+\partial_b\lambda$ for smooth $\lambda$. Its one-particle coefficient $g_h$ is the vector $g_j$ of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] for $j_i=-\partial_a h^{ai}$, so $F(h)=a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h)$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

Let $C_0=-i\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ is the massless scalar causal commutator of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. As distributions in $x-y$,
$$[E_i(x),E_j(y)]=[B_i(x),B_j(y)] =(-\delta_{ij}\Delta+\partial_i\partial_j)C_0(x-y),$$
$$[E_i(x),B_j(y)]=\epsilon_{jri}\partial_0\partial_rC_0(x-y).$$
Every right-hand side has support in the closed causal cone. Hence compactly supported tests whose supports are spacelike separated in the stated Minkowski sense give commuting field-strength operators on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The quotient representation of [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]] makes these smeared field strengths Lorentz covariant: their on-shell coefficient depends on a polarization class only through $p_a\epsilon_b-p_b\epsilon_a$.
